title: Systems of Linear Equations
summary: Students learn three systematic ways to solve two‑variable linear systems: substitution, elimination, and graphing. They practice each method with clear, step‑by‑step examples.
objectives: Apply the substitution method to find the solution of a two‑variable system
Use the elimination method to solve a two‑variable system
Graph two linear equations and locate their intersection point
Choose the most efficient method for a given system
Check solutions by substituting back into the original equations
prerequisites: Students should already know how to solve single linear equations and plot points on a coordinate plane.
why: Linear systems model real‑world situations such as budgeting, mixing ingredients, and determining break‑even points. Being able to solve them lets you predict outcomes when two quantities depend on each other.

The three methods give flexibility: substitution works well when one equation is already solved for a variable, elimination is fast for coefficients that line up, and graphing provides a visual check. Mastery builds a strong foundation for algebra, physics, economics, and engineering.

sections.heading: What Is a System of Linear Equations?
sections.body:
A **system of linear equations** is simply a group of two (or more) equations that we want to satisfy at the same time.  
Each equation in the group is called a *linear equation* because its graph is a straight line.  
When we look for a **solution** of the system, we are looking for a pair of numbers \((x, y)\) that makes **every** equation true together.

> **Definition:** A solution of a system of linear equations is a point \((x, y)\) that satisfies each equation in the system simultaneously.

Why does this idea matter?  Imagine each equation as a road on a map.  The road is straight because the equation is linear.  The point where all the roads meet is the place where you can be on every road at once – that is exactly the solution of the system.  If the roads never cross, there is no common point and the system has **no solution**.  If the roads lie on top of each other, every point on the line works, and the system has **infinitely many solutions**.

To see the picture, write the two equations in the usual form  

$$
a_1x + b_1y = c_1, \qquad a_2x + b_2y = c_2 .
$$  

Each equation can be drawn on the same set of axes.  The first line is the set of all points that satisfy the first equation, the second line is the set of points that satisfy the second.  Their intersection (if any) is the solution.

> **In daily life:** Think of two schedules: one says “the bus arrives at 8 am + 5 minutes per stop”, the other says “the train leaves at 8 am + 3 minutes per stop”.  The stop where both arrive at the same time is the intersection of the two lines – the solution of the schedule system.

There are three standard ways to find that intersection algebraically, without having to draw the lines:

1. **Substitution method** – solve one equation for a variable (say \(y\)) and replace it in the other equation.  This turns the second equation into a single‑variable equation, which is easy to solve.

2. **Elimination method (matching coefficients)** – add or subtract the equations after multiplying one or both by suitable numbers, so that one variable cancels out.  The remaining equation contains only one variable, which we solve first, then back‑substitute.

3. **Graphing method** – actually draw both lines on graph paper (or using a computer) and read off the point where they cross.  This visual approach shows the meaning of the solution clearly, but it is less precise when the intersection is not at nice integer coordinates.

> **Note:** All three methods give the same answer when the system has a unique solution; they just take different routes to get there.

Choosing the best method depends on the numbers involved.  If one equation is already solved for a variable, substitution is quick.  If the coefficients are small integers that line up nicely, elimination often requires only a little arithmetic.  If you are just starting out or want to check your work, graphing gives a helpful picture.

> **Remember:** A system can have one solution (the lines cross at a single point), no solution (parallel lines), or infinitely many solutions (the same line written twice).  Recognising which case you are in helps you decide whether to keep solving or stop early.

sections.heading: Substitution Method – Simple Form
sections.body:
When we talk about a **system of linear equations**, we mean two (or more) straight‑line equations that share the same variables.  
The **substitution method** solves the system by first expressing one variable in terms of the other from one equation, then putting that expression into the second equation. This turns the second equation into a single‑variable equation, which we can solve directly. After we find that variable, we substitute back to obtain the value of the remaining variable.

> **Definition:** *Substitution method* – a step‑by‑step process:  
> 1. Solve one equation for a variable.  
> 2. Substitute that expression into the other equation.  
> 3. Solve the resulting single‑variable equation.  
> 4. Back‑substitute to find the other variable.

Why does this work? Each equation tells us a relationship that must be true for the same pair \((x,y)\). If we rewrite one relationship so that it gives the exact value of \(x\) (or \(y\)) in terms of the other, we can replace the same variable in the second relationship. The two equations are now combined into one, so the only unknown left is the one we substituted for. Solving it gives a number that automatically satisfies both original equations.

Think of it like a recipe: one instruction tells you how much flour you need based on the amount of sugar, and another tells you the total weight of flour plus sugar. If you first write “flour = total – sugar”, you can plug that into the first instruction and find the exact amount of sugar, then work back to the flour amount. The same idea applies to algebraic equations.

---

**Example 1 (Easy):** Solve the system  
\[
\begin{cases}
x + y = 7 \\
x - y = 1
\end{cases}
\]

1. **Choose an equation to solve for a variable.**  
   From the first equation, isolate \(x\):  
   $$x = 7 - y$$

2. **Substitute this expression for \(x\) into the second equation.**  
   Replace \(x\) in \(x - y = 1\):  
   $$ (7 - y) - y = 1 $$

3. **Solve the single‑variable equation for \(y\).**  
   Simplify:  
   $$7 - 2y = 1$$  
   Subtract 7 from both sides:  
   $$-2y = -6$$  
   Divide by \(-2\):  
   $$y = 3$$

4. **Back‑substitute to find \(x\).**  
   Use \(x = 7 - y\):  
   $$x = 7 - 3 = 4$$

**Answer:** The solution is \((x, y) = (4,\;3)\). Both equations are satisfied.

---

**Example 2 (Medium):** Solve the system  
\[
\begin{cases}
2x + 3y = 12 \\
y = 4 - x
\end{cases}
\]

1. **Solve the second equation for \(y\).**  
   It is already solved:  
   $$y = 4 - x$$

2. **Substitute this expression for \(y\) into the first equation.**  
   Replace \(y\) in \(2x + 3y = 12\):  
   $$2x + 3(4 - x) = 12$$

3. **Simplify and solve for \(x\).**  
   Distribute the 3:  
   $$2x + 12 - 3x = 12$$  
   Combine like terms:  
   $$-x + 12 = 12$$  
   Subtract 12:  
   $$-x = 0$$  
   Multiply by \(-1\):  
   $$x = 0$$

4. **Back‑substitute to obtain \(y\).**  
   Use \(y = 4 - x\):  
   $$y = 4 - 0 = 4$$

**Answer:** The solution is \((x, y) = (0,\;4)\).  

> **Note:** When the second equation is already solved for a variable, the substitution step becomes a simple replacement, saving time.

---

### Why the method is useful

- **Clarity:** Each step isolates a single unknown, making algebraic manipulation straightforward.
- **Flexibility:** Works equally well for systems with any number of variables, as long as one equation can be solved for one variable.
- **Connection to real life:** In budgeting, you might know total cost and the cost of one item; solving for the unknown item’s price follows the same pattern.

> **In daily life:** If you know the total price of a meal (say \$25) and the price of the drink (\$5), you can find the price of the food by subtracting: food = total – drink. This is exactly the substitution idea.

---

### Things to watch out for

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to replace *every* occurrence of the variable in the second equation. In Example 2, the term \(3y\) becomes \(3(4 - x)\); missing the parentheses would give an incorrect equation.

> **Remember:** Always simplify after substitution before solving. This prevents algebraic errors and keeps the work tidy.

By following these clear, ordered steps, the substitution method turns a pair of linked equations into a single, easy‑to‑solve problem, then quickly gives the complete solution to the original system.

sections.heading: Elimination Method – Matching Coefficients
sections.body:
When we use the **elimination method**, we try to “cancel out’’ one of the variables by making its coefficient the same (or opposite) in the two equations.  
If the coefficients are the same, we can add the equations; if they are opposite, we can subtract them.  
The result is a single equation that contains only one unknown, which we can solve immediately.  

> **Definition:** *Elimination* means adding or subtracting whole equations after we have multiplied them by suitable numbers so that the coefficients of one variable match (or become opposites).

Why does this work?  
Each equation tells us a relationship that must be true for the same pair \((x,y)\).  
If we add two true statements, the sum is also true. By arranging the equations so that the \(y\)-terms (for example) cancel, the sum leaves only an equation in \(x\). Solving that gives the exact value of \(x\); we then substitute back to find \(y\).  

Think of it like a kitchen scale: you have two piles of fruit that together weigh the same as a third pile. If you know the weight of one type of fruit in each pile, you can “eliminate’’ that fruit by adding the piles, leaving only the weight of the other fruit to compare.

---

### Step‑by‑step procedure  

1. **Identify** which variable you want to eliminate.  
2. **Multiply** one or both equations by numbers that make the coefficients of that variable equal (or opposite).  
3. **Add** the equations if the coefficients are opposite, or **subtract** if they are the same.  
4. **Solve** the resulting single‑variable equation.  
5. **Substitute** the found value back into one of the original equations to obtain the other variable.  
6. **Check** the solution in both original equations.

> **Note:** Always simplify the multiplied equations before adding or subtracting; this avoids arithmetic errors.

---

#### **Example 3 (Easy):** Solving a pair with opposite \(y\) coefficients  

Solve the system  

\[
\begin{cases}
3x + 2y = 16\\
3x - 2y = 4
\end{cases}
\]

**Step 1 – Choose a variable to eliminate**  
The coefficients of \(y\) are already opposites (\(+2\) and \(-2\)), so we can add the equations directly.

**Step 2 – Add the equations**  

$$ (3x + 2y) + (3x - 2y) = 16 + 4 $$  

The \(2y\) and \(-2y\) cancel:

$$ 6x = 20 $$

**Step 3 – Solve for \(x\)**  

$$ x = \frac{20}{6} = \frac{10}{3} $$

**Step 4 – Substitute \(x\) back to find \(y\)**  
Use the first original equation:

$$ 3\left(\frac{10}{3}\right) + 2y = 16 $$  

Simplify:

$$ 10 + 2y = 16 $$  

$$ 2y = 6 $$  

$$ y = 3 $$

**Answer:** The solution is \((x, y) = \left(\dfrac{10}{3},\; 3\right)\). Both equations are satisfied.

---

#### **Example 4 (Medium):** Eliminating \(y\) after scaling  

Solve the system  

\[
\begin{cases}
4x + 5y = 20\\
2x - 5y = -6
\end{cases}
\]

**Step 1 – Choose a variable to eliminate**  
The coefficients of \(y\) are \(+5\) and \(-5\); they are already opposites, so we can add the equations without any multiplication.

**Step 2 – Add the equations**  

$$ (4x + 5y) + (2x - 5y) = 20 + (-6) $$  

The \(5y\) terms cancel:

$$ 6x = 14 $$

**Step 3 – Solve for \(x\)**  

$$ x = \frac{14}{6} = \frac{7}{3} $$

**Step 4 – Substitute \(x\) back to find \(y\)**  
Insert \(x = \dfrac{7}{3}\) into the second original equation (the one with the smaller coefficient for \(x\) to keep arithmetic simple):

$$ 2\left(\frac{7}{3}\right) - 5y = -6 $$  

$$ \frac{14}{3} - 5y = -6 $$  

Move the fraction to the right:

$$ -5y = -6 - \frac{14}{3} $$  

Write \(-6\) as \(-\dfrac{18}{3}\):

$$ -5y = -\frac{18}{3} - \frac{14}{3} = -\frac{32}{3} $$  

Divide by \(-5\):

$$ y = \frac{32}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{5} = \frac{32}{15} $$

**Answer:** The solution is \((x, y) = \left(\dfrac{7}{3},\; \dfrac{32}{15}\right)\). Substituting these values into both original equations confirms they are correct.

> **Remember:** After elimination you always have a single‑variable equation. Solving it first and then back‑substituting keeps the work organized and reduces mistakes.

---

### When elimination is especially useful  

- The coefficients of one variable are already the same or exact opposites (as in the examples).  
- Multiplying to match coefficients is simple (small integers).  
- You want to avoid fractions early; sometimes choosing the variable that leads to integer multipliers is smarter.

> **In daily life:** Imagine you have two recipes that use the same amount of sugar but opposite amounts of flour. By adding the recipes, the sugar amounts double while the flour cancels, leaving you with a clear picture of the total flour needed from other ingredients. The same idea lets us “cancel’’ a variable in algebra.

By mastering elimination, you gain a fast, reliable tool for solving linear systems, especially when the numbers line up nicely. Practice with different coefficient patterns, and you’ll quickly see which variable to eliminate for the smoothest calculation.

sections.heading: Graphing Method – Visual Intersection
sections.body:
When we talk about the **graphing method**, we are using a picture to solve a system of linear equations.  
Each equation describes a straight line on the coordinate plane.  
If the two lines cross, the point where they meet – the *intersection point* – gives the values of the variables that satisfy **both** equations at the same time.  

> **Definition:** A *system of linear equations* is a set of two or more linear equations that share the same variables.  
> **Note:** The graphing method works best when the lines are not parallel (they must have different slopes) and when the intersection point has nice, whole‑number coordinates that are easy to read from the graph.  

### Step 1 – Write each equation in slope‑intercept form  

The *slope‑intercept form* of a line is  

$$
y = mx + b
$$  

where $m$ is the **slope** (how steep the line is) and $b$ is the **y‑intercept** (the point where the line crosses the $y$‑axis).  
Re‑arranging an equation into this form makes it simple to plot: we just need two points – the intercept $(0,b)$ and another point found by using the slope.

### Step 2 – Plot the two lines  

1. Mark the $y$‑intercept on the vertical axis.  
2. From that point, move up (or down) and right according to the slope $m$ (rise over run).  
3. Draw a straight line through the points; repeat for the second equation.  

### Step 3 – Read the intersection  

Where the two drawn lines cross, drop a vertical line to the $x$‑axis and a horizontal line to the $y$‑axis.  
The coordinates of that crossing point are the solution $(x,\;y)$ of the system.

---

**Example 5 (Easy): Graph $y = 2x + 1$ and $y = -x + 4$**  

We want the point that satisfies both equations.

1. **Put both equations in slope‑intercept form.**  
   They are already in that form, so we identify the slopes and intercepts:  

   $$y = 2x + 1 \quad (m_1 = 2,\; b_1 = 1)$$  
   $$y = -x + 4 \quad (m_2 = -1,\; b_2 = 4)$$  

2. **Plot the first line.**  
   - Start at $(0,1)$.  
   - Slope $2$ means rise $2$ and run $1$: go up 2 units, right 1 unit to $(1,3)$.  
   - Draw the line through $(0,1)$ and $(1,3)$.  

3. **Plot the second line.**  
   - Start at $(0,4)$.  
   - Slope $-1$ means rise $-1$ and run $1$: go down 1 unit, right 1 unit to $(1,3)$.  
   - Draw the line through $(0,4)$ and $(1,3)$.  

4. **Find the intersection.**  
   Both lines pass through the point $(1,3)$.  

**Answer:** The system’s solution is $(x,\;y) = (1,\;3)$.  

---

**Example 6 (Medium): Graph $2x + y = 6$ and $x - 2y = -3$**  

We will solve this system by graphing.

1. **Rewrite each equation in slope‑intercept form.**  

   For $2x + y = 6$:  

   $$y = -2x + 6$$  

   Here $m_1 = -2$, $b_1 = 6$.  

   For $x - 2y = -3$: first isolate $y$:  

   $$-2y = -x - 3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y = \frac{1}{2}x + \frac{3}{2}$$  

   So $m_2 = \tfrac12$, $b_2 = \tfrac32$.  

2. **Plot the first line $y = -2x + 6$.**  
   - Intercept at $(0,6)$.  
   - Slope $-2$ means down 2, right 1: another point $(1,4)$.  
   - Draw the line through these points.  

3. **Plot the second line $y = \tfrac12 x + \tfrac32$.**  
   - Intercept at $\bigl(0,\tfrac32\bigr)$.  
   - Slope $\tfrac12$ means up 1, right 2: another point $(2, \tfrac32 + 1) = (2, \tfrac52)$.  
   - Draw the line through the two points.  

4. **Read the intersection.**  
   Looking at the sketch, the lines cross near $x = 2$ and $y = 2$.  
   To be precise, we can check the point $(2,2)$ in both original equations:  

   - $2(2) + 2 = 6 \;\checkmark$  
   - $2 - 2(2) = -2 \neq -3$ → not exact, so we refine.  

   From the graph we see the intersection is at $x = \frac{9}{5}$ and $y = \frac{12}{5}$.  
   Verify:  

   $$2\left(\frac{9}{5}\right) + \frac{12}{5} = \frac{18}{5} + \frac{12}{5} = \frac{30}{5} = 6$$  
   $$\frac{9}{5} - 2\left(\frac{12}{5}\right) = \frac{9}{5} - \frac{24}{5} = -\frac{15}{5} = -3$$  

   Both hold, confirming the point.  

**Answer:** The solution is $\displaystyle\left(x,\;y\right)=\left(\frac{9}{5},\;\frac{12}{5}\right)$ (approximately $(1.8,\;2.4)$).  

> **In daily life:** Imagine two roads on a map. Each road follows a straight line described by an equation. The place where the roads meet is the intersection – just like the solution to the system.  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to convert the equations fully into slope‑intercept form can lead to plotting the wrong slope or intercept, which moves the line and gives an incorrect intersection.  

By turning each equation into the easy‑to‑draw $y = mx + b$ shape, sketching the lines, and reading where they cross, the graphing method gives a visual and intuitive way to solve a system of linear equations. It is especially handy when you need a quick estimate or when you want to see how the two relationships interact on the same set of axes.

sections.heading: Choosing the Best Method
sections.body:
When you have a system of two linear equations, you can solve it in three different ways: substitution, elimination, or graphing.  
Each method works, but some are quicker or clearer depending on the numbers that appear in the equations.  
Below we compare the three techniques, point out when one is usually the best choice, and practice deciding which tool to pick.

> **Note:** A *system of linear equations* is a set of two (or more) equations that are all straight‑line equations; the solution is the pair \((x,y)\) that makes **every** equation true at the same time.

### 1. Substitution – best when a variable is already isolated  
If one of the equations already has a variable by itself, for example \(y = 3x + 2\) or \(x = 5\), you can simply replace that variable in the other equation.  
Because you are “substituting” a simple expression, you avoid extra algebraic work.

**Everyday comparison:** Imagine you already know the price of a single apple (the isolated variable). To find the total cost of a basket, you just plug that price into the basket‑price formula—no need to rearrange the basket formula first.

### 2. Elimination – best when coefficients line up nicely  
Elimination works by adding or subtracting the equations so that one variable disappears.  
It is most efficient when the coefficients (the numbers in front of \(x\) or \(y\)) are already the same or exact opposites, or when a small multiple makes them match.

**Everyday comparison:** Think of two piles of bricks. If one pile has exactly the same number of red bricks as the other, you can remove the red bricks from both piles at once, leaving only the other colors to compare.

### 3. Graphing – best for visual checks or when coefficients are small  
Graphing draws each equation as a straight line on the coordinate plane; the point where the lines cross is the solution.  
It is handy when you want a quick visual confirmation or when the coefficients are small enough to plot easily by hand.

**Everyday comparison:** It is like looking at two roads on a map; the intersection tells you where the two routes meet.

---

## How to pick the right method

1. **Look for an isolated variable.**  
   If either equation already solves for \(x\) or \(y\), choose substitution.

2. **Check the coefficients.**  
   - If a coefficient of \(x\) (or \(y\)) in one equation is a simple multiple of the same coefficient in the other, elimination will cancel that variable with little extra work.  
   - If the coefficients are messy or require large multipliers, elimination may create big numbers, so consider substitution instead.

3. **Consider the size of numbers for graphing.**  
   When the slopes and intercepts are small (e.g., \(\pm1, \pm2\)), plotting is fast.  
   With large or fractional coefficients, graphing becomes cumbersome and error‑prone.

4. **Think about the goal.**  
   If you need an exact algebraic answer (as in most exams), prefer substitution or elimination.  
   If you only need to know whether a solution exists or want a rough estimate, graphing is fine.

> **In daily life:** Choosing the right method is like picking the shortest route on a GPS—sometimes the straight highway (elimination) is fastest, sometimes a side street with a clear sign (substitution) saves you from traffic, and sometimes you just look at the map to see where two roads cross (graphing).

---

### Worked example – deciding the best method

**Example 7 (Hard): Choose the easiest method for the system**  
\[
\begin{cases}
5x - 2y = 9\\[2mm]
10x - 4y = 18
\end{cases}
\]

The question asks us to decide which method avoids unnecessary work and then solve the system.

1. **Inspect the equations.**  
   The second equation is exactly twice the first: every coefficient and the constant term are multiplied by 2.  
   This tells us that the two lines are *parallel* (they have the same slope) and will either coincide or have no intersection.

2. **Choose elimination.**  
   Because the coefficients of both \(x\) and \(y\) already match a simple multiple, we can eliminate a variable without any extra multiplication.

3. **Subtract the first equation from the second (or divide the second by 2).**  
   $$10x - 4y - (5x - 2y) = 18 - 9$$  
   Simplify:  
   $$5x - 2y = 9$$  

   Notice that after subtraction we obtain exactly the same equation we started with. This means the two equations are not independent; they represent the same line.

4. **Interpret the result.**  
   Since both equations describe the same line, there are infinitely many solutions that satisfy both. Any pair \((x,y)\) that makes \(5x - 2y = 9\) true will work.

5. **Write the solution set.**  
   Solve for one variable to describe the line:  
   $$5x - 2y = 9 \;\Longrightarrow\; y = \frac{5}{2}x - \frac{9}{2}$$  
   So the solution set is all points \((x,\,\frac{5}{2}x - \frac{9}{2})\).

**Answer:** The system has infinitely many solutions; it represents a single line \(y = \frac{5}{2}x - \frac{9}{2}\). Elimination was the quickest choice because the second equation was a multiple of the first, revealing the redundancy instantly.

---

### Quick checklist for future problems

- **Is a variable already alone?** → *Substitution*  
- **Do coefficients line up with a small multiple?** → *Elimination*  
- **Are numbers tiny and you want a picture?** → *Graphing*  
- **If two equations look proportional, check for redundancy first** – you may discover “infinitely many” or “no” solutions without heavy algebra.

> **Remember:** The goal is to reach the answer with the least extra work. Scanning the equations first saves time and reduces mistakes.

sections.heading: Checking Your Answers
sections.body:
When we finish solving a system of linear equations, the last thing we should do is **check our answers**.  
In plain words, checking means putting the numbers we found for the variables back into each original equation to see if the statements become true.  

Why do we do this?  
If we made an arithmetic slip, chose the wrong sign, or mixed up the equations, the numbers we obtained will not satisfy every equation. By substituting them back, we catch those errors before we move on.  

Think of it like a recipe: after you bake a cake, you taste a small piece to be sure it turned out right. The “taste test” for algebra is the substitution step.

---

> **Note:** *Substituting* means replacing a variable (like $x$ or $y$) with the value you have found, and then simplifying the left‑hand side (LHS) of the equation. If the LHS equals the right‑hand side (RHS), the equation is satisfied.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to substitute the value into **both** equations, or only checking one side of an equation. Always verify every original equation.

> **Remember:** If a solution works in all equations, it is a *valid solution* for the system.

### Worked example

**Example 8 (Easy): Verify the solution \((3,4)\) for \(x + y = 7\) and \(2x - y = 2\).**  

We have already solved the system and obtained $x=3$, $y=4$. Now we check each equation.

1. **Substitute into the first equation** $x + y = 7$.  
   Replace $x$ with $3$ and $y$ with $4$:
   $$
   3 + 4 = 7
   $$
   The left‑hand side simplifies to $7$, which equals the right‑hand side $7$. The first equation is satisfied.

2. **Substitute into the second equation** $2x - y = 2$.  
   Replace $x$ with $3$ and $y$ with $4$:
   $$
   2(3) - 4 = 2
   $$
   Simplify:
   $$
   6 - 4 = 2
   $$
   The left‑hand side becomes $2$, matching the right‑hand side $2$. The second equation is also satisfied.

3. **Conclude** that the pair \((3,4)\) works for both equations, so it is indeed the correct solution.

**Answer:** The solution \((x,y) = (3,4)\) satisfies both original equations; therefore it is correct.

---

### Step‑by‑step checklist for any system

1. **Write down each original equation** exactly as it was given.  
2. **Replace every variable** with the value you found.  
3. **Simplify** the left‑hand side using ordinary arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division).  
4. **Compare** the simplified left‑hand side with the right‑hand side.  
   - If they are equal for **all** equations, the solution is correct.  
   - If any equation fails, revisit your work: look for sign errors, misplaced terms, or arithmetic slips.

> **Definition:** A *valid solution* to a system of linear equations is a set of numbers that makes **every** equation in the system true when substituted.

> **In daily life:** Imagine you have two different maps that both claim to show the same treasure location. You check the coordinates on each map; only if both maps point to the same spot can you be confident you have the right place. Substituting checks that both “maps” (equations) agree on the same “coordinates” (solution).

### Why checking matters even with different methods

You might have solved the system by substitution, elimination, or graphing. Each method involves different algebraic manipulations, and each is prone to its own typical errors:

- **Substitution** can lead to sign mistakes when moving terms.  
- **Elimination** may cause arithmetic errors when adding or subtracting multiples of equations.  
- **Graphing** can suffer from rounding errors when reading coordinates off a graph.

Regardless of the method, the substitution check is a universal safety net.

### A quick tip for larger systems

When a system has three or more variables, the same idea applies: substitute the found values into **each** original equation. If any equation does not hold, the solution set is incomplete or incorrect.

---

> **Note:** If you obtain a *fraction* or *decimal* while checking, keep the same level of precision you used when solving. Rounding too early can make a correct solution appear wrong.

### Final thought

Checking your answers is not an optional afterthought; it is an integral part of problem solving. It reinforces the logical structure of algebra: a solution must satisfy **all** conditions imposed by the system. By habitually performing this step, you develop confidence in your work and reduce the chance of carrying forward a mistake.

---

practice.q: Solve the system using substitution: \[ \begin{cases} x + 2y = 8\\ y = 3 \end{cases} \]
practice.a:
From the second equation we already have \(y = 3\). Substitute into the first:
\(x + 2(3) = 8 \Rightarrow x + 6 = 8 \Rightarrow x = 2\).
Solution: \((2,3)\).

Add the two equations to eliminate \(y\):
\((4x+4x) + (5y-5y) = 20 + 0 \Rightarrow 8x = 20 \Rightarrow x = \frac{20}{8}= \frac{5}{2}\).
Substitute \(x = \frac{5}{2}\) into the second equation:
\(4\left(\frac{5}{2}\right) - 5y = 0 \Rightarrow 10 - 5y = 0 \Rightarrow 5y = 10 \Rightarrow y = 2\).
Solution: \(\left(\frac{5}{2}, 2\right)\).

practice.q: Use substitution to solve: \[ \begin{cases} 3x - y = 4\\ 2x + y = 7 \end{cases} \]
practice.a:
Add the two equations to eliminate \(y\):
\((3x - y) + (2x + y) = 4 + 7 \Rightarrow 5x = 11 \Rightarrow x = \frac{11}{5}\).
Substitute into the second equation:
\(2\left(\frac{11}{5}\right) + y = 7 \Rightarrow \frac{22}{5} + y = 7\).
\(y = 7 - \frac{22}{5} = \frac{35 - 22}{5} = \frac{13}{5}\).
Solution: \(\left(\frac{11}{5}, \frac{13}{5}\right)\).

First make the coefficients of \(y\) opposites. Multiply the second equation by 3:
\(12x - 9y = 6\).
Now add to the first equation:
\((6x + 12x) + (9y - 9y) = 45 + 6 \Rightarrow 18x = 51 \Rightarrow x = \frac{51}{18}= \frac{17}{6}\).
Substitute \(x = \frac{17}{6}\) into the second original equation:
\(4\left(\frac{17}{6}\right) - 3y = 2 \Rightarrow \frac{68}{6} - 3y = 2\).
Simplify \(\frac{68}{6}= \frac{34}{3}\).
\(\frac{34}{3} - 3y = 2 \Rightarrow -3y = 2 - \frac{34}{3}= \frac{6 - 34}{3}= -\frac{28}{3}\).
\(y = \frac{-28/3}{-3}= \frac{28}{9}\).
Solution: \(\left(\frac{17}{6}, \frac{28}{9}\right)\).

practice.q: A system models a small business: \[ \begin{cases} 5a + 2b = 23\\ 3a - 4b = -1 \end{cases} \] Solve using elimination and verify the solution.
practice.a:
Choose to eliminate \(a\). Multiply the first equation by 3 and the second by 5:
\(15a + 6b = 69\)
\(15a - 20b = -5\)
Subtract the second from the first:
\((15a-15a) + (6b + 20b) = 69 - (-5) \Rightarrow 26b = 74 \Rightarrow b = \frac{74}{26}= \frac{37}{13}= 2.\!846\) (keep as fraction \(b = \frac{37}{13}\)).
Now substitute \(b\) back into the first original equation:
\(5a + 2\left(\frac{37}{13}\right) = 23\)
\(5a + \frac{74}{13} = 23\)
Convert 23 to thirteenths: \(23 = \frac{299}{13}\).
\(5a = \frac{299}{13} - \frac{74}{13}= \frac{225}{13}\)
\(a = \frac{225}{13}\times\frac{1}{5}= \frac{225}{65}= \frac{45}{13}= 3.\!4615\).
**Check:**
First equation: \(5a + 2b = 5\left(\frac{45}{13}\right) + 2\left(\frac{37}{13}\right)= \frac{225}{13} + \frac{74}{13}= \frac{299}{13}=23\) ✓
Second equation: \(3a - 4b = 3\left(\frac{45}{13}\right) - 4\left(\frac{37}{13}\right)= \frac{135}{13} - \frac{148}{13}= -\frac{13}{13}= -1\) ✓
Solution: \(\displaystyle\left(a,b\right)=\left(\frac{45}{13},\frac{37}{13}\right)\).

practice.q: A linear‑programming style problem gives the equations: \[ \begin{cases} 2x + 3y = 12\\ 4x - y = 5 \end{cases} \] Use the substitution method, then explain why this solution also represents the intersection point of the two lines on a graph.
practice.a:
Solve the second equation for \(y\):
\(-y = 5 - 4x \Rightarrow y = 4x - 5\).
Substitute into the first equation:
\(2x + 3(4x - 5) = 12\)
\(2x + 12x - 15 = 12\)
\(14x = 27 \Rightarrow x = \frac{27}{14}\).
Find \(y\):
\(y = 4\left(\frac{27}{14}\right) - 5 = \frac{108}{14} - 5 = \frac{108}{14} - \frac{70}{14}= \frac{38}{14}= \frac{19}{7}\).
**Verification:**
First equation: \(2\left(\frac{27}{14}\right) + 3\left(\frac{19}{7}\right)= \frac{54}{14} + \frac{57}{7}= \frac{54}{14} + \frac{114}{14}= \frac{168}{14}=12\) ✓
Second equation: \(4\left(\frac{27}{14}\right) - \frac{19}{7}= \frac{108}{14} - \frac{38}{14}= \frac{70}{14}=5\) ✓
**Why it is the intersection:**
Each equation describes a straight line in the \(xy\)-plane. Solving the system finds the unique ordered pair \(\left(\frac{27}{14},\frac{19}{7}\right)\) that satisfies **both** equations simultaneously. Geometrically, this pair is the point where the two lines cross; no other point lies on both lines, so the algebraic solution equals the graphical intersection.

recap: A system of linear equations is a set of two or more straight‑line equations that must be true at the same time. You can solve the system by substitution, elimination, or graphing, each turning the problem into a single‑variable equation. After finding the values, always check them by plugging back into the original equations.

key_terms.meaning: A group of two or more linear equations that share the same variables and must be satisfied together.
A pair (x, y) that makes every equation in the system true.
Solve one equation for a variable, replace that expression in the other equation, solve for the remaining variable, then back‑substitute.
Add or subtract whole equations after scaling them so that one variable cancels out, leaving a single‑variable equation.
Draw each equation as a line on a coordinate plane; the intersection point gives the solution.
An equation written as y = m x + b, where m is the slope and b is the y‑intercept.
When the lines are parallel and never intersect, the system has no common point.
When the equations represent the same line, every point on the line satisfies the system.

quiz.q: What does a solution of a system of linear equations represent?
options: A pair (x, y) that satisfies all equations
quiz.why: A solution is the point that makes every equation true simultaneously.

quiz.q: Which method is best when one equation already has y isolated?
quiz.why: Substitution directly replaces the isolated variable into the other equation.

quiz.q: In elimination, what do you do to cancel a variable?
options: Multiply one equation by a number then add or subtract
quiz.why: You scale the equations so the coefficients match or are opposites, then add or subtract to cancel.

quiz.q: If two lines are parallel, the system has:
quiz.why: Parallel lines never intersect, so there is no common point.

quiz.q: What is the slope‑intercept form of a line?
quiz.why: Slope‑intercept form expresses y in terms of x with slope m and intercept b.

quiz.q: When checking your answer, you should:
options: Plug the values back into the original equations
quiz.why: Substituting the found values verifies they satisfy each original equation.
